After recently using Rufus to install the Ubunto ISO to a stick, I went through a puzzling and problematic install from the thumb drive. Before I succeeded, I had reached my wit's end as to the source. Yes, I was reformatting the USB stick on ISO transfer.

Booting from the stick, the hardware probing would start; FAULTY_READ errors cascaded on my screen for almost thirty seconds before it advanced. I tried different options (Install Ubuntu, Try Live Ubuntu, etc.) and it still crashed during the installation. Then it came to me.

Solution: Age of stick! The thumb drive hadn't been used for long period of time.

Using Rufus, I reinstalled the ISO to the thumb drive. This time I also checked "Check for Bad Sectors". Voila! It went smoothly.

If one has erratic errors when using a stick, reformat the drive and check for bad sectors.

I've had a lot of similar problems with USB sticks and other storage devices.. I've pretty much got to the point where I've decided it's not worth going cheap. It just costs more pain and money down the road. I've just been screwed way too many times by cheap usb sticks/SD cards/hardrives. I always try to research before I buy now.

This kind of corruption can happen with any media btw. It can be actual bad blocks, or just plain old data rot.

BTRFS has a scrub feature that works in conjunction with its data checksum feature to read and check the checksum of all data chunks on storage media. When there is mirroring, as in the case of raid 1 or 10, then the hope is that the other copy will have a good read and the bad data can be replaced.

This does pretty much the same thing that checking for bad blocks does, with the exception that you can use the device while it's doing it.
